paper_metadata.title: Implementing Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (qGAN) and QCBM in Finance

experiments.description: Hybrid qGAN experiment for learning a real-world Binance-based financial distribution for option-pricing uncertainty using a quantum generator and classical discriminator.

algorithm.variant: qGAN with variational quantum generator and classical binary discriminator
algorithm.ansatz: multi-layer variational quantum circuit with single- and two-qubit gates; layers composed of RX/RZ rotations and controlled entangling gates
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained for 2000 epochs; equilibrium discussed when generator and discriminator losses intersect

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Five crypto-asset features were discretized with 3 qubits per feature, giving 32 discrete values per feature; training samples were mapped to discrete values after percentile trimming.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize discriminator loss L_D = -1/(|X|+|S|) [sum_x log D_phi(x) + sum_s log(1 - D_phi(G_theta(s)))] and generator loss L_G = -1/|S| sum_s log(D_phi(G_theta(s)))
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Percentile trimming of samples below 5% and above 95% to reduce required qubits / discretization range

problem_instance.description: Option-pricing uncertainty modeling / distribution learning from Binance crypto-market data.
problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Histogram-based discretization verification was performed; PyTorch tensors and data loader were created from the training data.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Loss curves and fidelity evolution were inspected during training; no explicit cross-validation or repeated-run protocol reported.

classical_preprocessing: discretize features according to qubit resolution

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: generator and discriminator losses intersect near Nash equilibrium; fidelity increases with iterations

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states that qGAN produced expected results in far fewer iterations than a classical GAN, but no numerical classical baseline, runtime, or speedup factor is reported.

experiments.description: QCBM experiment for learning a financial probability distribution from the same Binance dataset using a 5-layer quantum circuit and comparing optimizers.

algorithm.ansatz: interleaved layered quantum circuit with repeated odd/even layer structure
algorithm.convergence_criteria: optimization of cost function over 5 layers; no explicit stopping threshold reported
algorithm.parameter_initialization: parameters initialized for variational optimization; exact initialization not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: A parametrized quantum circuit was trained to approximate the target probability distribution P(x) = |<x|psi(theta)>|^2 over the dataset; exact qubit-to-variable mapping not explicitly stated.
problem_formulation.objective_function: C(theta) = -(1/d) sum_{d=1}^{5} ln(P(x_d)); variant used C(theta) = -(1/d) sum_{d=1}^{5} ln(max(epsilon, P_theta(x_d)))
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: max(epsilon, P_theta(x_d)) regularization to avoid log(0)

problem_instance.description: Distribution learning / generative modeling on Binance crypto-market data.

preprocessing: histogram generation to verify state-vector characteristics
use of the same Binance dataset as qGAN experiment

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: A histogram was generated to verify that the state vector satisfies the target distribution characteristics; no further preprocessing details reported.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Optimizer comparison across COBYLA, SPSA, and Nelder-Mead; comparison of simulated distribution against real distribution, with SPSA appearing close to the real data.

classical_preprocessing: generate histogram to inspect target distribution
classical_postprocessing: compare simulated distribution with real distribution

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper compares optimizers qualitatively and states that COBYLA was marginally better than SPSA, but no numerical optimizer scores, runtime, or speedup factor are reported.
